summary: Methotrexate is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor (folate antimetabolite) used both as antineoplastic chemotherapy and, at much lower WEEKLY doses, as a disease-modifying agent for rheumatoid arthritis, polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and severe psoriasis. It carries boxed warnings for embryo-fetal toxicity (contraindicated in pregnancy for non-neoplastic disease), severe hypersensitivity, and serious/fatal adverse reactions of the bone marrow, GI tract, liver, lungs, skin, and kidneys. A critical safety point is that in rheumatologic and dermatologic use methotrexate is dosed ONCE WEEKLY - inadvertent daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity. Folic or folinic acid supplementation reduces toxicity in non-oncologic use, and leucovorin (with glucarpidase for impaired clearance) is the rescue agent in overdose.
indications: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in adults and pediatric patients, as part of a combination chemotherapy maintenance regimen
Mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma) in adults, as a single agent or part of combination chemotherapy
Relapsed or refractory non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults, as part of a metronomic combination regimen
Other neoplastic uses (per broader methotrexate labeling): gestational trophoblastic disease/choriocarcinoma, breast cancer, head and neck cancer, and lung cancer
Polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (pJIA) in pediatric patients
Severe, recalcitrant, disabling psoriasis unresponsive to other therapy

admin: WEEKLY DOSING ALERT: for rheumatoid arthritis, pJIA, and psoriasis, methotrexate is taken ONCE PER WEEK, not daily. Daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity. Confirm the day and frequency with every patient and caregiver.
Instruct patients and caregivers to take exactly as directed - medication errors have led to deaths
Verify pregnancy status in females of reproductive potential before starting
Do not give tablets to patients unable to swallow a tablet; switching from oral to IV/IM/SC may require an alternative dosing regimen
Methotrexate is a cytotoxic drug - follow applicable special handling and disposal procedures
Co-administer folic acid or folinic acid as directed to reduce adverse reactions in non-neoplastic use (do not start folate supplements on your own in neoplastic use - it can reduce efficacy)
Monitor blood counts, liver, and renal function at baseline and periodically; withhold/reduce/discontinue for significant toxicity
moa: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolic acid reductase (dihydrofolate reductase). Dihydrofolates must be reduced to tetrahydrofolates by this enzyme before serving as carriers of one-carbon groups in the synthesis of purine nucleotides and thymidylate. By blocking this step, methotrexate interferes with DNA synthesis, repair, and cellular replication. Actively proliferating tissues - malignant cells, bone marrow, fetal cells, and buccal/intestinal mucosa - are most sensitive. The precise mechanism of benefit in rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis is unknown but is thought to involve anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects.

absolute: Pregnancy in patients receiving methotrexate for non-neoplastic (non-malignant) diseases - embryo-fetal toxicity including fetal death (BOXED WARNING)
History of severe hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, to methotrexate (BOXED WARNING)
relative: Pre-existing significant hepatic impairment or chronic liver disease / alcoholism
Significant renal impairment (delayed clearance, increased toxicity)
Pre-existing blood dyscrasias or significant myelosuppression
Peptic ulcer disease or ulcerative colitis (higher risk of severe GI toxicity)
Third-space fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion) - delays clearance, increases toxicity
monitor: Pregnancy test in females of reproductive potential before initiation
CBC with differential and platelets at baseline and periodically
Liver function tests (and consider liver imaging/biopsy with long-term use)
Signs of infection, pulmonary symptoms (cough, dyspnea), mucositis/stomatitis, and skin reactions

preg: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy for non-neoplastic (non-malignant) diseases (BOXED WARNING). Based on published reports and its mechanism of action, methotrexate causes embryo-fetal toxicity and fetal death. First-trimester exposure is linked to spontaneous abortion and malformations (skull anomalies, facial dysmorphism, CNS and limb abnormalities, and sometimes cardiac anomalies and intellectual impairment); second/third-trimester exposure can cause intrauterine growth restriction and functional abnormalities. In one prospective study of women taking <=30 mg/week after conception, the spontaneous abortion/miscarriage rate was 42%. Verify pregnancy status before starting. Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 6 months after the final dose, and advise males with female partners of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 months after the final dose. For neoplastic disease, advise pregnant patients of the potential risk to the fetus. Because methotrexate persists in tissues, there is risk even from preconception exposure.
lact: Methotrexate is present in human milk in low amounts (highest reported milk-to-plasma ratio ~0.08:1). Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed child, instruct women NOT to breastfeed during treatment with methotrexate and for 1 week after the final dose.
renal: Methotrexate is primarily eliminated renally by glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion. The elimination half-life is variable and increases with the severity of renal impairment, raising toxicity risk. Reduce the dose and monitor closely in renal impairment; avoid or use great caution with significant impairment, and maintain adequate hydration. Nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, probenecid, etc.) can further increase methotrexate exposure.
hepatic: Methotrexate can cause severe and potentially irreversible hepatotoxicity, including fibrosis, cirrhosis, and fatal liver failure (BOXED WARNING). Elevated liver tests occurred in ~15% of rheumatoid arthritis patients in short-term studies. The effect of hepatic impairment on methotrexate pharmacokinetics is unknown. Avoid in significant hepatic disease or alcoholism; obtain LFTs at baseline and periodically, and consider liver imaging/biopsy with prolonged use. Withhold or discontinue for clinically significant hepatotoxicity.

major: NSAIDs and aspirin/salicylates - reduce renal clearance and increase methotrexate exposure/toxicity (especially with high-dose MTX); monitor closely
Nephrotoxic drugs - additive renal injury and delayed clearance, increasing toxicity
Probenecid - decreases renal tubular secretion, markedly raising methotrexate levels
Nitrous oxide anesthesia - potentiates effects on folate-dependent pathways; avoid, and consider alternatives in patients with prior nitrous oxide exposure
Antifolate drugs (e.g., dapsone, pemetrexed, pyrimethamine, sulfonamides/trimethoprim) - additive antifolate toxicity, severe myelosuppression
Live vaccines - not recommended due to immunosuppression
moderate: Oral antibiotics including penicillins, sulfonamides, and neomycin - can increase methotrexate plasma concentrations
Proton pump inhibitors - can increase and prolong methotrexate (and 7-OH metabolite) levels
Highly protein-bound drugs (oral anticoagulants, phenytoin, salicylates, sulfonamides, sulfonylureas, tetracyclines) - displace methotrexate, raising free levels
minor: Theophylline - methotrexate may decrease theophylline clearance; monitor levels
interactions.food: Food delays absorption and reduces peak concentration; take consistently with respect to meals. Folic/folinic acid taken as directed reduces non-oncologic toxicity but can reduce methotrexate efficacy in neoplastic disease, so take folate only as instructed by the prescriber.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive hepatotoxicity and increased risk of cirrhosis/liver fibrosis.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor CBC with platelets, liver function tests, and serum creatinine/renal function at baseline and periodically. Monitor serum methotrexate levels in high-dose regimens and overdose.

serious: Myelosuppression - severe, life-threatening pancytopenia, anemia, leukopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia (BOXED WARNING)
Hepatotoxicity - fibrosis, cirrhosis, fatal liver failure (BOXED WARNING)
Pulmonary toxicity - interstitial pneumonitis, which can be fatal
Severe GI toxicity - hemorrhagic enteritis, intestinal perforation (can be fatal)
Renal toxicity / acute renal failure (especially high-dose)
Serious infections, including opportunistic infections (can be fatal)
Tumor lysis syndrome in patients at risk
rare: Severe dermatologic reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, exfoliative dermatitis)
Neurotoxicity (including with intrathecal use - leukoencephalopathy, seizures)
Secondary malignancies, including malignant lymphomas (may regress on withdrawal)
emergency: Signs of severe bone marrow suppression - high fever, severe sore throat, unusual bleeding/bruising, profound fatigue (medical emergency)
Embryo-fetal harm if taken in pregnancy - discontinue immediately and obtain urgent obstetric evaluation
New or worsening cough, dyspnea, or fever (pneumonitis) - stop drug and seek care
Severe diarrhea, mucositis, or GI bleeding (risk of perforation)
Signs of anaphylaxis or severe skin reaction (blistering, peeling)
Suspected overdose or inadvertent daily dosing - seek emergency care (leucovorin rescue)

monitoring: CBC with differential and platelet count at baseline, periodically during treatment, and as clinically indicated
Liver function tests at baseline and periodically; consider liver imaging/biopsy with long-term use
Serum creatinine / renal function (and serum methotrexate levels in high-dose regimens)
Pregnancy test before initiation in females of reproductive potential
Pulmonary symptoms (cough, dyspnea, fever) suggestive of pneumonitis
Signs of infection, mucositis/stomatitis, and dermatologic reactions
In high-dose/risk settings: tumor lysis labs (uric acid, K, phosphate, Ca), hydration and urinary alkalinization
counsel: TAKE ONCE A WEEK, NOT DAILY (for arthritis/psoriasis). Taking methotrexate every day by mistake can be fatal. Know your dose and the exact day you take it; consider marking the day on a calendar.
Take folic or folinic acid exactly as your prescriber directs to lower side effects - do not start or stop folate on your own
Do not get pregnant - methotrexate causes severe birth defects and miscarriage; use effective contraception during treatment and after stopping (6 months for women, 3 months for men)
Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 1 week after the last dose
Avoid alcohol to protect your liver
Report immediately: fever, sore throat, unusual bleeding/bruising, mouth sores, cough or shortness of breath, severe diarrhea, or yellowing of skin/eyes
Avoid taking NSAIDs/aspirin and starting new medicines without checking, and avoid live vaccines
Keep all blood test appointments to monitor blood counts, liver, and kidneys
pk: RA response usually at 3-6 weeks (up to 12 weeks); antineoplastic effect per cell cycle
Plasma peak 0.75-6 hours after oral dosing; food delays and lowers peak
Elimination half-life ~3 to 10 hours; increases with renal impairment
Active polyglutamate metabolites retained in tissues for prolonged periods
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions 15-30 C permitted; cytotoxic - special handling
pearls: WEEKLY, NOT DAILY: for RA, pJIA, and psoriasis methotrexate is dosed ONCE WEEKLY. Inadvertent daily dosing is a classic, sometimes fatal, prescribing/dispensing error - always confirm frequency and day.

Three core boxed warnings: embryo-fetal toxicity (contraindicated in pregnancy for non-neoplastic disease), severe hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis, and serious/fatal toxicity of marrow, GI tract, liver, lungs, skin, and kidneys.
Folic or folinic acid supplementation reduces toxicity (mucositis, GI, hepatic, hematologic) in non-oncologic use without abolishing efficacy; in neoplastic use, folate can reduce efficacy.
Leucovorin (folinic acid) is the rescue antidote for toxicity/overdose; glucarpidase rapidly lowers toxic methotrexate levels in patients with impaired renal clearance.
RA doses >20 mg once weekly substantially increase serious adverse reactions including myelosuppression.
Third-space fluid (ascites, pleural effusion) acts as a methotrexate reservoir, delaying clearance and increasing toxicity - drain or dose-adjust and monitor.
missed: For ONCE-WEEKLY (arthritis/psoriasis) dosing: if a weekly dose is missed, contact the prescriber; generally take it as soon as remembered if it is within a day or two, then resume the regular weekly schedule. NEVER take two weekly doses close together or take methotrexate on consecutive days to make up a missed dose - this can cause severe, potentially fatal toxicity. Never switch to daily dosing. For oncologic regimens, follow the specific protocol and oncology team instructions for missed doses.
overdose: Overdose, including fatal overdose, has occurred - frequently from inadvertent DAILY dosing of a once-weekly regimen. Manifestations are mainly hematologic and GI: leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, pancytopenia, myelosuppression, mucositis/stomatitis, oral ulceration, nausea, vomiting, GI ulceration or bleeding; sepsis/septic shock, renal failure, and aplastic anemia have been reported. Management: administer LEUCOVORIN (folinic acid) or levoleucovorin as soon as possible after overdose, guided by serum creatinine and methotrexate levels. GLUCARPIDASE is indicated for toxic plasma methotrexate concentrations (>1 micromole/L) in patients with delayed clearance due to impaired renal function. Give concomitant hydration and urinary alkalinization. Hemodialysis/peritoneal dialysis are not reliably effective, though high-flux intermittent hemodialysis has cleared methotrexate in some cases.
